parts.note: goods travel as parcels, so trips taken the way goods go are trips made as a bundled parcel

explanation.surface: A question about outings made by freight train.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goods' suggests a goods train; the parcels that goods travel in name the all-inclusive holiday.
explanation.definitionFit: Holiday trips sold as an all-in bundle of travel and lodging are named after a parcel.

definitions.meaning: Peregrine is the hero of Tobias Smollett's novel The Adventures of Peregrine Pickle

explanation.surface: A falcon kept for posterity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peregrine' suggests the falcon, but it is the hero of Smollett's 1751 novel 'Peregrine Pickle'.
explanation.definitionFit: Food steeped in vinegar is kept this way, and Smollett's hero Peregrine bore the matching surname.

clue.text: Spellbinder from whom a lady refused a drink at the Castle

definitions.text: Spellbinder from whom a lady refused a drink at the Castle

parts.words: Spellbinder from whom a lady refused a drink at the Castle
parts.note: the enchanter in Milton's masque, first performed at Ludlow Castle, who offers the virtuous Lady a magic cup she refuses

explanation.surface: An enchanter's charmed drink is turned down by a lady in a castle.
explanation.walkthrough: Milton's 1634 masque, performed at Ludlow Castle, has the sorcerer offer the Lady his enchanted cup, which she refuses.
explanation.definitionFit: Milton's enchanter, son of Bacchus and Circe, is the title figure of the Ludlow Castle masque.

parts.note: a staff in Exodus turned into a serpent, and the same name is given to tall garden plants such as mullein

explanation.surface: A question about the gardeners in a winding park.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Garden staff' looks like gardeners; it is the rod of Moses' brother, which became a snake before Pharaoh, and also a cottage-garden plant (mullein or goldenrod).
explanation.definitionFit: The biblical rod that turned into a snake gives its name to tall spiky garden plants.

clue.text: Some that put down 'roots in Chelmsford

indicators.note: in says the answer sits inside the word that follows, Chelmsford

explanation.surface: Some people have settled and made their home in an Essex town.
explanation.walkthrough: Chelmsford is the county town of Essex; the trees sit inside its letters. 'Some that put down roots' sounds like settlers, but it is trees.
explanation.definitionFit: Trees put down roots, and these are one familiar kind of broadleaf tree.

parts.note: read over-wound as spread over a cut or sore rather than wound too tightly like a clock spring

explanation.walkthrough: 'Over-wound' suggests a watch spring wound too far; split it as 'over wound' (rhyming with 'tuned') and it is a salve put on an injury.
explanation.definitionFit: A medicated salve or cream is something spread on a sore or cut.

parts.note: read 'up against it' as risen up in opposition rather than in difficulties

explanation.walkthrough: 'Up against it' usually means in trouble; read literally it is someone who has risen in revolt against authority.
explanation.definitionFit: An insurgent is someone who rises in arms against the established power.

clue.text: At this a gun doesn't knock one all of a heap

definitions.text: At this a gun doesn't knock one all of a heap

parts.words: At this a gun doesn't knock one all of a heap
parts.note: a firearm set at its safety position cannot fire, so it cannot surprise or floor anyone

explanation.surface: A gun that fails to overwhelm someone.
explanation.walkthrough: With the hammer at the safety position a gun cannot fire, so 'going off' this way means acting too soon and achieving nothing. 'All of a heap' means astonished.
explanation.definitionFit: The safety position of a gun's hammer, half raised, from which it cannot be fired.

parts.note: a barrier built to break up waves, which are called breakers

explanation.walkthrough: Breakers are large waves; the low sea wall built out from a beach to check them is a breaker of breakers.
explanation.definitionFit: A low wall run out into the sea to check the waves and stop the beach washing away.

clue.text: Arrived a fellow from the Academy for some shooting

parts.note: came is the past tense of arrive at, so arrived means came
RA stands for the Royal Academy (and its members, Royal Academicians)
a fellow is a man

explanation.surface: A newcomer from the art academy turns up to join a hunting party.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces go CAME, then RA, then MAN, so the clue's 'a fellow' comes after the Academy in the answer. 'Shooting' is filming, not hunting.
explanation.definitionFit: A film crew member operating the camera is the person employed to shoot the scenes.

parts.note: the quotation marks make Grave a title: the eighteenth-century Scottish poem The Grave and the man who wrote it

explanation.walkthrough: Robert Blair (1699-1746) wrote the long poem 'The Grave', the founding work of the so-called graveyard poets; the quotation marks stop 'Grave' being an adjective for a solemn poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Blair was the Scottish author of the meditative poem The Grave.

indicators.note: something cryptic is obscure and jumbled, so the letters before it are to be scrambled

parts.note: the 's stands for 'is', but its S is also a letter of the fodder

explanation.surface: Someone complains that the jargon is puzzling and earns nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cryptic' rearranges LINGOS (lingo plus the S of 'lingo's') into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A venture that is unprofitable is one making a loss rather than gaining money.

parts.note: a slump is poor trade; at a chippy that means only a little frying is done, a tiny amount fried

explanation.surface: A bad week for the local chippy.
explanation.walkthrough: A fish-and-chip shop is a British takeaway where fish is deep-fried; slack trade there means the frying is small. The phrase also means young fish and, figuratively, unimportant people.
explanation.definitionFit: Small fry are tiny young fish, and the phrase is also used for people of no importance.

clue.text: It is not meet so to do

definitions.text: It is not meet so to do

parts.words: It is not meet so to do
parts.note: read 'meet' as the verb 'come together' rather than the old adjective 'fitting': the opposite of meeting is going away

explanation.surface: A solemn, old-fashioned pronouncement that some action would be improper.
explanation.walkthrough: The archaic 'it is not meet' means 'it is not proper', but here 'meet' is the verb: to leave is the opposite of to meet.
explanation.definitionFit: To leave or go away is the reverse of coming together with someone.

definitions.meaning: the load line painted on a ship's hull, showing how low she may safely sit in the water
rubber-soled canvas sports shoes, named for that line because of the band round their sides

explanation.surface: A safety rule printed inside some footwear.
explanation.walkthrough: In British English these are also the canvas gym shoes, so called for the line of rubber round them.
explanation.definitionFit: Samuel Plimsoll's load mark on hulls lent its name to canvas gym footwear with a rubber band.

clue.text: What's ahead that's likely to turn up ?

definitions.text: What's ahead that's likely to turn up ?

parts.words: What's ahead that's likely to turn up ?
parts.note: 'what's ahead' is what sits at the front of the head, a feature that tends to tilt upward

explanation.surface: A question about what the future might bring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What's ahead' sounds like the future and 'turn up' like something arriving; read literally they are a feature at the front of the face that points upward.
explanation.definitionFit: A short nose with an upturned tip is described by this term.

definitions.meaning: an 1854 Crimean War battle, site of the Charge of the Light Brigade
a knitted woollen helmet covering the head and neck, named after the battle

explanation.surface: A war fought over fleece.
explanation.walkthrough: The Crimean War battle gave its name to the knitted hood sent to troops there.
explanation.definitionFit: The Crimean battle shares its name with the woollen head-covering soldiers wore.

clue.text: Tortoise trying to prevent Continental drift ?

definitions.text: Tortoise trying to prevent Continental drift ?

parts.words: Tortoise trying to prevent Continental drift ?
parts.note: Latin terra is the earth, and pinning the earth down would stop the continents drifting

explanation.surface: A slow reptile attempting to halt the movement of tectonic plates.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as TERRA (Latin for earth) and PIN: something to fix the ground in place, against continental drift. The animal is a freshwater turtle, loosely a tortoise.
explanation.definitionFit: A small freshwater turtle, which loosely counts as a tortoise.

clue.text: This has a traditional pull at Christmas, with ribbons attached

definitions.text: This has a traditional pull at Christmas, with ribbons attached

parts.words: This has a traditional pull at Christmas, with ribbons attached
parts.note: the pull is hauling a sleigh, and ribbons is old slang for the reins a draught animal wears

explanation.surface: A Christmas cracker, pulled at the festive table and tied with ribbons.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a Christmas cracker; in fact the animal that pulls Father Christmas's sleigh, harnessed with reins ('ribbons' is old coaching slang for reins).
explanation.definitionFit: Santa's sleigh is drawn by antlered Arctic deer in the Christmas tradition.

clue.text: As concerns fighting a penny is the pay

parts.note: re, from Latin, means concerning or about
war is fighting
D is the abbreviation for a penny in old British money (from Latin denarius)

explanation.surface: A soldier's wages amount to a single penny.
explanation.walkthrough: Before 1971 British pennies were written d, from Latin denarius.
explanation.definitionFit: A payment given in return for work or service is a recompense.

parts.note: a thirst satisfied is one this word describes, and the same word names the lime of builders treated with water

explanation.surface: A thirsty drinker refreshed with a lime juice.
explanation.walkthrough: A lime drink seems to quench thirst; but 'slaked lime' is quicklime that has been treated with water, so the lime is the chemical, not the fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: A thirst that is quenched has been satisfied, and lime combined with water is called by the same word.

parts.note: read course as a stage of a meal, so the spoon belonging to a particular course

explanation.walkthrough: 'Of course' looks like 'naturally'; it is a meal course, and the spoon used for the sweet one.
explanation.definitionFit: The sweet course of a meal gives its name to a medium spoon used for it.

parts.note: read sage as wise and tractarian as a fellow of a tract of land, a piece of ground measured in acres

explanation.surface: A wise member of the Oxford Movement.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tractarians were the Oxford Movement churchmen; here 'tract' is a piece of land, an acre, after 'sage' = wise. The word means a know-all, so the 'sage' is ironic.
explanation.definitionFit: A know-all who pretends to great learning is mockingly given this name.

parts.note: the ancient Assyrian capital shared its name with the chief Assyrian deity

explanation.walkthrough: The city on the Tigris and the supreme Assyrian god (also spelt Ashur) share the name.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient Assyrian capital on the Tigris was named after the nation's chief deity.

clue.text: Dick's car, Estelle, is somewhat frightening

indicators.note: somewhat says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Someone finds Dick's car a bit alarming, Estelle.
explanation.definitionFit: Frightening someone, as a verb, is alarming them, as the answer does.

parts.note: a Fleming here is a woman surnamed Fleming, heroine of a George Meredith novel, put into a book

explanation.surface: A Flemish person made to answer for wrongdoing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brought to book' usually means punished; here it means put into a book. Meredith's 1865 novel is 'Rhoda Fleming', and 'a Fleming' is not a native of Flanders.
explanation.definitionFit: Meredith titled a novel after its heroine, a farmer's daughter called Fleming.

parts.note: Wordsworth's poem ...-Leap Well tells of a stag that leapt to its death beside a spring

explanation.walkthrough: 'Leap well' looks like an instruction; it is part of the title 'Hart-Leap Well', the Wordsworth poem about a hunted stag, so the missing first word is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A male deer, the stag whose fatal leap names Wordsworth's poem.

definitions.text: There were gardens bright with sinuous" (Coleridge

parts.words: There were gardens bright with sinuous" (Coleridge
parts.note: the blank is the missing last word of the line from Kubla Khan, a word for small winding streams

explanation.walkthrough: The line in Kubla Khan runs 'And there were gardens bright with sinuous ___'; the missing word is plural for little brooks.
explanation.definitionFit: Small streams or brooks are what the poet's sinuous gardens were bright with.

clue.text: Start to pen with Harry a line to a bird

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter, here of pen

parts.note: Hal is the nickname of Prince Harry in Shakespeare's Henry IV
a rope is a line on a ship

explanation.surface: Instructions to begin writing a line with Harry about a bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Start to' gives the first letter of 'pen'; Prince Hal is Shakespeare's young Henry V.
explanation.definitionFit: A small wading bird of the sandpiper family, notable for females courting males.

parts.note: a mill's work is turning and crushing grain, so mills that stop cease their crushing

explanation.walkthrough: Mills grind, so the phrase for stopping gradually reads literally as a mill finishing its work.
explanation.definitionFit: To come slowly to a standstill is the idiom here, pictured as a millstone ceasing.
